description: Before coffee, before breakfast, test your legs cold. The morning jump test shows what your nervous system brings to the first hour, then see what a daily morning stair ritual does in week one, week two and week four to your leg power and your whole day.

scenes.narration: Tomorrow morning, before coffee, before breakfast, run this test. Stand next to a wall, reach up, and mark your highest touch. Then jump, reach, and mark again. The gap between the two marks is your number, your cold morning jump. No warm-up, no second try. This is the honest one, the jump your nervous system owns before the day talks it into anything. Keep the number. A morning stair ritual is about to raise it, and at the end I will tell you what your cold jump says about your leg power.

scenes.label: ON A COLD MORNING JUMP IS THE LINE
scenes.narration: Here is the line. Thirty centimeters on a cold, first-thing jump means your legs wake up with real spring in them. Under twenty, your mornings start with the parking brake on, and that is most people. Over forty five, your nervous system reports for duty like an athlete's. The cold number is lower than your warm gym number, and that gap is exactly what this habit closes.
scenes.sub: under 20 cm: parking brake on - over 45 cm: elite spring

scenes.narration: Week one, the ritual feels rude. Legs are heavy, the stairs are steep, the bed was warm. But something shifts by day four: you reach the top and realize you are awake in a way coffee used to fake. The morning grogginess that normally eats your first hour gets spent on the stairs instead. Your cold jump creeps up a centimeter or two. Not because your legs grew. Because the signal from brain to muscle stopped arriving late.

Week two, the stairs stop being an alarm clock and start being a charger. Week four, you retest cold, and the jump that started the month is suddenly five, six, seven centimeters higher. That is not a warm-up effect, because the test is cold. Your legs genuinely report for duty stronger. And the carryover is the real prize: first steps out the door feel springy, hills feel shorter, and the whole day runs on legs that were switched on before breakfast.

lines: Cold muscle is not weak muscle.
beats.title: IT IS THE SIGNAL

scenes.narration: Here is the mechanism. A cold muscle is not a weak muscle. The contractile machinery is all there at 7 a.m. What is slow is the signal: your nervous system wakes up gradually, and early on it recruits your leg muscles timidly, a few fibers at a time. Climbing stairs first thing is a daily rehearsal of the opposite. Every step demands the full leg, right now, against gravity. Week after week, the morning signal gets faster and braver. That is why the cold jump rises. You did not just train legs. You trained the hour they wake up.
Climb with me for one minute. Steady steps, tall chest, wake the legs up one floor at a time. This is the ritual, right here. Go.

The protocol is about order. Stairs first, before coffee, before the phone, before your brain negotiates. One flight counts on the hard mornings; more is a bonus. Keep the pace steady and breathe through your nose on the way up. If you live somewhere flat, use a step, a curb, a sturdy box, one minute of step-ups in the doorway. The staircase is not the point. The point is that climbing is the first thing your legs do every day, so power becomes how your day starts, not how it ends.

So, your cold number. Under twenty centimeters: your legs start every day with the brake on, and this ritual is built for you. Twenty to thirty: average spring, one month from feeling genuinely different. Over thirty, cold: you own a morning most athletes would respect. Retest in thirty days, same wall, same cold legs, first thing. Put your centimeters in the comments. Just the number. Cold numbers do not lie, and yours is going up.

Wake your legs before you wake your phone. One climb, first thing, every day, and your mornings start with power instead of fog. Subscribe, and bring me your new cold jump in thirty days. This is {channel}. Train the cable.

title: Do This Every Morning: What stairs Does to Your leg power
